evidence: Collins and his brother Catfish, along with fellow J.B.'s member Frankie 'Kash' Waddy, joined Funkadelic in 1972 after leaving James Brown's band. Bootsy played bass on Funkadelic's mid-1970s albums and rejoined Clinton's Parliament for 'Up for the Down Stroke' (1974), co-writing its title track (widely documented, including in Collins's own memoir and interviews cited by Rolling Stone and NPR).

trackPair.whatToListenFor: 'The Grunt' is a J.B.'s instrumental built around a tight, repeating bass figure with almost no ornamentation. 'Up for the Down Stroke', four years and one J.B.'s walkout later, keeps that same repeating-figure discipline but stretches it, adds Bernie Worrell's synthesizer, and lets Collins's bass talk back to the vocals instead of just holding time.

explanation: After leaving James Brown's band, Bootsy Collins joined George Clinton's Funkadelic, then two years later helped write Parliament's first big hit for Casablanca Records, 'Up for the Down Stroke'. He carried Brown's disciplined rhythm section straight into Clinton's more experimental, synthesizer-heavy P-Funk sound, and 'Up for the Down Stroke' is usually named as the record where that mix first became a hit nobody could ignore.
